name: Candles
summary: Wax and liquid-paraffin candles: tea lights, church votives, tapers, pillars and glass-jar prayer and memorial candles. A little light and a little heat each, and a fire risk if left alone, near anything that burns, or burning while you sleep.
uses: Low light to sit by, awake: one candle is about 1 candela, roughly 12–13 lumens if it shone evenly all round (calculated), against about 800 lumens for a 60 W bulb (NIST candela, FEMP bulbs). In an outage a flashlight is safer (USFA candles, OFM candles)

A little heat: NIST measured about 77 W from one 21 mm paraffin taper (NIST candles), so ten would make about 770 W, from ten open flames in one room. A pot over candles adds no heat, and a house fire has followed trying it (AAP FactCheck)

Long steady burns from memorial and prayer candles sold as 3-day, 5-day and 6–7-day lights (Root church catalog); every candle still goes out before you sleep and when you leave the room (Health Canada candles)
Burn it in a sturdy holder that won't tip, away from curtains, bedding, clothing and decorations, and out of reach of children and pets (Health Canada candles)
Wax is fuel: NIST measured paraffin's heat of combustion at about 43.8 kJ per gram, roughly 12 kWh per kilogram (NIST candles)
identify: Burn times are makers' figures for a trimmed wick in still air; draughts and long wicks cut them. Tea lights (aluminium or plastic cup): IKEA lists 4 h for one pack and 6 h for another, and Root sells 4 h tea lights and 6 h disposable plastic lights (IKEA GLIMMA 100-pack, IKEA GLIMMA 36-pack, Root church catalog). Church pressed votives: 2 to 20 h, often numbered by their hours, so #10 is a 10-hour votive (Root church catalog). Tapers: a 25 cm (9 3/4 in) taper burns about 5.5 h (IKEA KLOKHET); NIST's 21 mm paraffin taper burned down about 2 cm (3/4 in) an hour and used about 6 g of wax an hour (NIST candles). Jar memorial and prayer candles: 3-day, 5-day and 6–7-day (Root church catalog). Root's plastic-cased 7-day cemetery candle melts if it burns, so it stands in a cemetery globe on a non-combustible surface (Root cemetery candle). Wax: paraffin is the commonest; beeswax, soy, palm, gel and blends burn in the same basic way (NCA FAQ), so size and wick matter more than the wax. Wicks with a metal core are made with zinc or tin today (NCA FAQ); a core that leaves a grey mark on white paper is probably lead (Health Canada candles).
test: Wick: there must be enough to light, and it should be fabric. If it has a metal core, pick the wax off the tip, separate the strands and rub the core on white paper: a grey mark suggests lead, so don't burn it (Health Canada candles). The US has banned wicks with more than 0.06% lead in the metal since October 2003 (CPSC candles). Canada's Candles Regulations only require that a candle not relight itself (Candles Regulations), and the Consumer Products Containing Lead Regulations do not cover candles (Lead Regulations); Health Canada says it works with the candle industry to end the sale and import of lead-core-wick candles (Health Canada candles), so check old and imported candles. Jar candles: look for cracks and chips in the glass, and stop with about 1 cm (1/2 in) of wax left; stop pillars and tapers with about 5 cm (2 in) left (NCA FAQ). Light it on a plate away from anything that burns and trim the wick to about 6 mm (1/4 in) (NCA FAQ, Health Canada candles). After the first few minutes the flame should be steady and not smoke; one that flickers or smokes is not burning properly: put it out, let it cool, trim the wick and move it out of the draught (NCA FAQ). Liquid-paraffin cartridges: check the bottle for cracks and the top for leaks before lighting. Health Canada warns that a child who reaches oil-lamp fuel (liquid paraffin) may swallow, breathe in or aspirate it, so keep cartridges out of reach (Health Canada oil lamps); if it is swallowed, don't make the person vomit (ISMP lamp oil). Melted or bent candles still burn: stand them in a sturdy holder on a non-combustible tray, since glass holders can crack when hot and wooden or plastic ones can burn (Health Canada candles).

decay.note: Estimate: wax keeps for years. Heat in a summer car, attic or shed softens or melts it; it still burns if stood in a jar. Plastic-bottle liquid candles can crack and leak.

improvise: For light, use a flashlight or battery lantern instead of a candle in a power outage (USFA candles, OFM candles); a 60 W bulb gives about 800 lumens against about 12 for a candle (FEMP bulbs, NIST candela). A wick lamp on lamp oil or kerosene does the same job with a steadier flame: see the wick lamp guide. For heat, a candle gives about 77 W (one 21 mm taper, NIST candles), so ten give under 800 W, from ten open flames in one room. Clay-pot candle heaters do not add heat: the pot only stops it rising to the ceiling, and a house fire has followed trying one (AAP FactCheck). For safe burning, holders, tea lights and what to do when one tips, see the guide 'Use candles in an outage without starting a fire'; for keeping warm, the staying warm guide.
